content: 1. When ethinylestradiol is coadministered with atazanavir/ritonavir, its exposure is decreased. Alternative or additional contraceptive measures are recommended to ensure contraceptive efficacy. 2. The effect of efavirenz on ethinylestradiol exposure depends on the hormonal contraceptive method used. No significant effect on ethinylestradiol exposure was observed with combined oral contraceptives containing ethinylestradiol/norgestimate. However, exposure was reduced when using a vaginal ring releasing etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol (120/15 µg/day). Progestogen levels were significantly decreased with both methods, and therefore, the use of efavirenz with these contraceptives is not recommended as it may compromise contraceptive efficacy. 3. Coadministration of atazanavir/ritonavir with a combined vaginal ring increased etonogestrel exposure but decreased ethinylestradiol exposure. Since dosage adjustment of ethinylestradiol is not possible with the vaginal ring, alternative contraceptive methods or additional barrier contraception should be used. 4. Efavirenz coadministration decreased levonorgestrel exposure. The Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare Clinical Guidance recommends the use of a copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) as the most effective emergency contraception for women on enzyme-inducing drugs. For women ineligible for Cu-IUD, a single dose of 3 mg levonorgestrel is recommended, supported by pharmacokinetic studies showing compensation for reduced levonorgestrel levels due to efavirenz induction. 5. Coadministration of efavirenz decreased the estrogen component of combined pills. Due to insufficient clinical data on contraceptive efficacy, caution is advised, and additional contraceptive measures should be used. 6. Efavirenz may reduce the contraceptive efficacy of norethisterone. Alternative contraceptive methods or additional measures are recommended. 7. Coadministration of efavirenz may decrease ulipristal exposure, potentially reducing the efficacy of emergency contraception pills. A copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) should be considered as an alternative. 8. Sildenafil exposure may increase with coadministration. It is recommended to use sildenafil cautiously at a reduced dose of 25 mg every 48 hours, with increased monitoring for adverse events. 9. Atazanavir exposure may decrease when coadministered with antacids. Atazanavir/ritonavir should be administered 2 hours before or 1 hour after antacids. 10. Rilpivirine exposure may decrease with antacid coadministration. Antacids should be taken at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. 11. Bictegravir should be taken at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after antacids containing aluminum or magnesium. Simultaneous administration with such antacids is not recommended. Bictegravir can be taken under fasting conditions 2 hours before antacids containing aluminum, magnesium, or calcium. 12. Dolutegravir exposure decreases with coadministration of medications containing polyvalent cations (e.g., antacids). Dolutegravir should be administered 2 hours before or 6 hours after such medications. Avoid coadministration in the presence of integrase class resistance. 13. Raltegravir exposure may decrease due to chelation by divalent metal cations. Coadministration with aluminum or magnesium antacids is not recommended. Calcium carbonate antacids should not be coadministered with once-daily raltegravir. If unavoidable, twice-daily raltegravir can be administered with calcium carbonate antacids. 14. Loperamide exposure may increase with coadministration, but opioid CNS effects are unlikely. Cardiac events, including QT interval prolongation, have been reported with high doses of loperamide. Caution is advised when using high doses, particularly in patients at risk of cardiac events due to electrolyte disturbances. 15. Atorvastatin exposure may substantially increase with coadministration and is not recommended. If necessary, the lowest possible dose of atorvastatin should be used, not exceeding 10 mg daily, with careful safety monitoring. 16. Pravastatin exposure may increase with coadministration. It is recommended to start with the lowest dose and titrate up to achieve the desired clinical effect while monitoring for safety. 17. Colchicine exposure may increase with coadministration. Refer to the product label for dose recommendations for gout flare treatment/prophylaxis and familial Mediterranean fever. Coadministration is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 18. Enhanced levodopa effects, including severe dyskinesia, have been reported with some protease inhibitors. Monitor for levodopa/carbidopa efficacy. 19. Dexamethasone concentrations may increase with coadministration, requiring dose adjustment. Careful monitoring for steroid-related adverse effects is recommended. Chronic or high doses of dexamethasone may decrease antiretroviral drug exposure, potentially leading to therapeutic failure and resistance development. Use with caution. 20. Coadministration may decrease dexamethasone concentrations. Doubling the dexamethasone dose is recommended when used in COVID-19 treatment. 21. Coadministration may increase comedication concentrations, necessitating dose adjustment. Careful monitoring for steroid-related adverse effects is recommended.
